title: Pandora and the box
subtitle: The jar of evils
subject: mythologie
description: The first woman made by the gods, Pandora opened a jar full of plagues. Hope stayed at the bottom. A myth about curiosity and misfortune.

hero.hook: It was not a box. It was a jar. And what it held changed the fate of every human being.

blocks.text: In Greek myth, **Pandora** is not only a character. She is the first woman, shaped by the gods as a trap. **Zeus** wanted to punish the humans who had received fire from [[Prometheus]].

Pandora arrived carrying a jar. When she opened it, she released the evils that ended human carelessness. One puzzling thing stayed at the bottom: **hope**. This is how the phrase “opening Pandora's box” was born.

After the theft of fire, Zeus ordered **Hephaestus**, god of the forge, to shape a woman out of clay and water, as beautiful as a goddess. Each Olympian added a gift. **Athena** taught her weaving. **Aphrodite** gave her charm. **Hermes**, messenger of the gods, slipped her cunning and lies.

blocks.caption: Pandora, “the one who received every gift”, created to deceive humankind

blocks.text: They named her **Pandora**: “the one who received every gift”. Prometheus had warned his brother **Epimetheus** to accept no present from Zeus. Too late. Epimetheus, the one who thinks afterward, fell for her charm and welcomed her in.
For the Greeks, Pandora was not created as a companion. She was designed as a punishment, a “beautiful evil” meant to strike humankind.

sections.title: The jar opens, the plagues fly out

blocks.text: Pandora carried a “pithos”, a large storage jar. Latin texts and modern translations would turn it into a “box”. Inside, the gods had locked away old age, sickness, famine, madness, and war.
The “box” mistake came from [[Erasmus of Rotterdam]] in the 16th century. While translating Hesiod, he mixed up “pithos” (a jar) and “pyxis” (a small casket).

Driven by the curiosity the gods had planted in her, Pandora lifted the lid. The evils escaped all at once. In a panic she shut the jar again. Too late. Only [[Elpis]], Hope, was left, clinging to the bottom.
Why did hope stay in the jar? People have argued about it since antiquity. If the container held nothing but evils, should we conclude that hope is one of them?
For some, like the philosopher **Nietzsche**, hope only stretches out the torment: it keeps us from accepting reality. For others, Zeus left it there on purpose, as the one remedy against despair.
In Greek, [[Elpis]] is not purely positive. The word means the expectation of what is coming, good or bad. A neutral force, able to save or to torment.

In **Hesiod**, author of the Theogony, the Pandora story carries a strong streak of [[misogyny]]: woman appears there as a burden on man. This myth has often been compared to Eve and the biblical fall.
In other versions, the jar held blessings. By flying off to Olympus, they became forever out of reach for mortals.

Later Pandora also became the figure of curiosity. Her disobedience let misfortune loose, but it also pushed humankind to work, invent, and survive. Today, “opening Pandora's box” means an action with consequences nobody can control.
The jar of **Pandora** ended human carelessness. The evils spread, and **hope** stayed at the bottom: the only counterweight to misfortune, and an ambiguous one.
